# Cursor confirms security breach led to malicious Claude Code extension

By

# Lawrence Abrams

- November 14, 2026

- 12:27 PM

- 0



Cursor confirmed it suffered a security breach that let hackers distribute a malicious Claude Code extension through its marketplace after stealing credentials from AI infrastructure provider Fireworks AI.



The breach also let attackers access internal systems and steal customer data, including historical AI coding-agent traces containing unredacted credentials that were later used to compromise additional services.



The breach was disclosed in a new incident report published Friday, which explains how attackers distributed malicious versions of Anthropic's Claude Code extension through Cursor's marketplace on October 29.



The attack exposed up to 5,000 developers to malware that installed persistent SSH backdoors.



Cursor is an AI-powered code editor built on Microsoft's open-source Visual Studio Code (VS Code), allowing developers to write, modify, and debug software using AI assistants.



According to Cursor, the attack began when hackers obtained an access key stored on Fireworks AI, a third-party provider used for AI model training and inference.



The attackers used the exposed key to copy data from a read-only storage bucket Cursor used to share information with Fireworks.



This bucket contained historical AI coding-agent traces, mostly from 2025, collected from users who had not enabled Privacy Mode and whose data could be used for model training. Some of these traces contained unredacted API credentials, allowing the attackers to access additional Cursor systems.



Cursor says fewer than 0.05% of users had coding-agent traces exposed, while fewer than 0.01% of customers had API credentials compromised.



Using the exposed credentials, the hackers stole data from several of Cursor's software-as-a-service (SaaS) tools, including:





- Archived, non-production Cursor source code repositories, some containing business contact information.


- Limited customer support information and email conversations.


- Product usage metrics and customer contact details.


- Summaries of some AI coding-agent conversations.


- Credentials that customers had previously shared with Cursor's support team.



Cursor says its monitoring systems detected the unauthorized activity, leading the company to revoke the Fireworks access key, rotate exposed credentials, and investigate additional unauthorized access.



As the investigation progressed, Cursor temporarily turned off some internal and product services as a precaution.



However, the attackers had already obtained a credential that allowed them to distribute extensions through Cursor's marketplace.



On October 29, the hackers used that credential to publish malicious copies of Anthropic's Claude Code extension on Cursor's VS Code extension marketplace.



"On October 29, using a stolen credential from the exposed data from our internal system, the attacker placed malicious, unauthorized copies of Anthropic's Claude Code extension directly on the cache used to serve the Cursor VS Code extension marketplace," Cursor explained.



The attack did not compromise Anthropic's legitimate extension or Open VSX, the extension marketplace Cursor uses.



The malicious extensions, versions 2.1.312 and 2.1.313, were available for approximately 11 hours before Cursor removed them.



As BleepingComputer previously reported , the attackers modified the legitimate Claude Code extension to execute malicious JavaScript that attempted to install persistent SSH backdoors on developers' computers.



The malware collected system information, installed an attacker-controlled SSH key, attempted to enable SSH access, and configured persistence mechanisms to maintain remote access.



However, security researchers found coding errors that likely prevented the backdoor from working on many Windows and macOS systems where SSH was not already enabled.



Cursor estimates that up to 5,000 users who requested affected extension versions during the exposure window may have received the malicious builds.



The company says its production infrastructure, official application releases, customer code repositories, and code and prompts belonging to users with Privacy Mode enabled were not affected.



Cursor says it has moved all inference traffic away from Fireworks, revoked and rotated exposed credentials, rebuilt its extension marketplace, and redeployed its production infrastructure as a precaution.



Customers who installed or updated to the affected Claude Code extension during the attack are advised to follow Cursor's remediation guidance .




# Black October


The incident comes amid a wave of attacks targeting AI developer platforms that cybersecurity company Wiz has dubbed "Black October" .



These attacks targeted development infrastructure to steal authentication credentials, especially those providing access to AI models.



Stolen credentials have been used for unauthorized AI inference, generating substantial charges for affected customers, with some incidents also linked to attempts at AI model distillation.



The attacks have affected numerous companies, including Railway , Northflank, Lightning AI, OpenCode , and Warp .



At Railway, attackers stole customer authentication secrets, which were later used to generate approximately $740,000 in fraudulent AI charges. OpenCode also reported exposed API keys and unauthorized AI usage.



Fireworks AI was also affected, disclosing multiple security breaches in October, including one involving exposed API keys and tokens and another in which attackers accessed development machines through a compromised third-party cloud provider.



The Fireworks incidents also affected other customers, including Notion , which recently disclosed that AI chat transcripts from a small number of workspaces were exposed.

import sys,re

    li=re.search(r'<link>(.*?)</link>',it,re.S)
    pd=re.search(r'<pubDate>(.*?)</pubDate>',it,re.S)
    print((pd.group(1) if pd else '?'),'|',(ti.group(1) if ti else '?'))
    print('   ',li.group(1) if li else '?')
"

# Elon Musk, other tech execs sign petition calling on Nvidia to reinstate Jensen Huang

A petition calling on Nvidia to reinstate the company’s recently ousted CEO Jensen Huang appears to have attracted more than 115,000 signatures as of Saturday afternoon.

The petition website said the signers include 5,965 current Nvidia employees, 1,108 former employees, and 63,063 shareholders. Notable supporters include Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, Replit CEO Amjad Masad, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan.

The petition states that its signers are “concerned that Jensen was removed without meaningful due process” and demands that the board “bring him back while an independent investigation establishes the facts.” It also calls on the board to ensure a fair investigation and provide more information to the public.

“Jensen deserves due process, not mob justice,” the petition says.

Huang resigned on Thursday , four days after confessing to having an affair with a chip executive suspected by U.S. intelligence to be a Chinese spy. The former CEO has agreed to testify before Congress, while news reports have also suggested that Huang engaged in multiple extramarital affairs .

Nvidia appointed CFO Colette Kress as the company’s interim CEO while it searches for a permanent replacement. Nvidia’s stock price fell sharply through the week, while Huang’s departure is also expected to leave a big gap in AI industry funding .

input.prompt: Give the publication date, the authors/organization, and all quantitative findings with exact numbers (apps scanned, records exposed, percentages).

response.result:
**Publication date:** The page does not state a publication date for the report. It references a Handelsblatt article by Lina Knees dated November 2, 2026, and notes that the report contains more recent figures than that article.

**Authors/organization:** Crissy Field GmbH (Hamburg), in collaboration with Handelsblatt. No individual report authors are named.

**Quantitative findings:**
- **Projects examined:** 159,041 Lovable projects (December 2025 to September 2026), drawn from Common Crawl.
- **Supabase users:** 34,545 of those projects used Supabase.
- **Unprotected on load:** 24,664 websites sent Supabase database records without login or other interaction.
- **Email-containing records:** Records with email addresses appeared in 10,560 tables across 7,403 of the 24,664 websites, or 30%.
- **Specific cases:**
  - A German lifestyle forum exposed more than 80,000 profiles and more than 200,000 chat messages.
  - A service provider exposed more than 1,000 records with identity document details, including passport numbers.
  - One provider's 280,000 sent emails to customers were accessible.
  - Event organizers and restaurants exposed tens of thousands of ticket and food sales records.

**Caveat:** The authors state that the 30% figure is not a confirmed data leak rate. It applies only to the 24,664 websites examined more closely, and the sample is not representative of all Lovable applications. The records retrieved were only partial downloads, so the affected datasets may contain more.

# Asian governments react to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s exit

Kate Park

8:34 AM PST · November 14, 2026

Jensen Huang’s departure from Nvidia has drawn a range of responses across Asia, with some governments moving to confirm chip supply commitments, while others are monitoring the impact on local projects or addressing ongoing investigations.

On Sunday, November 8, Nvidia’s board launched an independent investigation after reports that Huang was targeted by a Chinese spy operation; Huang admitted to an affair with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based chip company Megaspeed.

Nvidia’s influence extends far beyond the United States. The chip giant has built close ties with companies worldwide, particularly in Asia, where many of its key partners play important roles in the global AI industry.

# China

China’s foreign ministry rejected allegations on November 10 that a Chinese businesswoman linked to former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was a spy, calling them groundless and a smear against Beijing. On Friday , a spokesperson reiterated opposition to export controls that disrupt global supply chains and stated the ministry was not aware of reports linking restricted Nvidia chips to a Shanghai data center associated with Alice Huang.

Huang’s exit has also raised uncertainty over more than $3 billion in Chinese AI computing projects reliant on Nvidia’s restricted processors, according to Reuters. Many of these chips are subject to U.S. export controls, making them difficult for Chinese companies to obtain.

# Singapore

In Singapore, authorities seized the passport of Alice Huang, former CEO of Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed, in June 2025 as part of an investigation into possible false declarations regarding server purchases, according to the Ministry of Home Affairs.

The Singapore ministry said police took her passport to ensure she remained available for questioning, as she was not based in Singapore. The investigation examined whether servers shipped from Singapore to Malaysia were later sent to other countries without proper declaration.

In February 2026, police found insufficient evidence to establish that Alice Huang had committed offenses related to the suspected false declarations, according to the ministry. However, authorities said she had knowingly provided inaccurate information about her role at Megaspeed. She was issued a warning and barred from re-entering Singapore. Her passport was returned that month. Singapore also said it received limited assistance from U.S. authorities despite repeated requests for information about U.S. server maker Supermicro. Singapore’s Ministry of Home Affairs said its investigation into Megaspeed and six other individuals remains ongoing. The ministry did not identify the six individuals or specify their alleged roles in the case.

# South Korea

South Korea has close ties to Nvidia, with major chipmakers Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix playing important roles in supplying memory chips used in its AI processors. response.result:
**Publication:** "Will We Really Put Data Centers in Space?" by Avi Parrack and Fin Moorhouse, Forethought, dated 22 May 2026.

**Core finding:** The cost case for orbital data centers (ODCs) "depends almost entirely on Starship achieving reusability" comparable to Falcon.

**Key quantitative findings**

*Energy and launch cost*
- Dawn-dusk sun-synchronous solar panels produce roughly 3–5× the energy of the same panel at a good terrestrial site.
- Space solar reaches cost parity with present-day off-grid terrestrial power at roughly $250/kg to orbit.
- It becomes cheaper than any current terrestrial source at around $50/kg, where it could fall to $25–45/MWh.
- Present launch cost is roughly $1,500/kg. The authors say ODCs approach cost parity with terrestrial builds at about $100/kg, a 15× reduction.

*Five-year cost per GW (IT hardware held at $25.6B/GW)*

| Scenario | $B per 5-yr cycle |
|---|---|
| Earth Grid | 37.6 |
| Earth Microgrid (Conservative) | 42.5 |
| Earth Microgrid (Bullish) | 36.8 |
| ODC (Conservative, $250/kg) | 48.2 |
| ODC (Median, $100/kg) | 35.0 |
| ODC (Bullish, $50/kg) | 30.3 |

*Cooling*
- Passive radiators could reach about 163–346 W/kg at system level, versus about 13 W/kg for ISS-era radiators (13–28× improvement).
- Thermal hardware is about 2–5% of total ODC cost.

*Reliability*
- The model assumes a 9% annual compute loss from chips that cannot be swapped, which requires about 38% extra non-IT hardware over 5 years.
- Meta's 16,384-GPU H100 cluster logged 419 hardware failures in 54 days.

*Launch economics (Starship, $90M build cost)*
- Per-kg cost falls from about $475 (expendable) to about $51 (Falcon-like full reuse) and about $19 (bullish, 100 reuses).

*Scaling and timing*
- Slow scenario: about 4 GW of orbital compute by 2031, against a forecast of about 100 GW of terrestrial buildout by 2030.
- Fast scenario: up to 100 GW of orbital compute operational by end of 2030.
- Current FAA approval caps Starship at 145 launches per year (about 0.5 GW/yr), which would need roughly a 35-fold increase.

*Bandwidth and radiation*
- Commercial inter-satellite optical links run about 1–100 Gbps, which likely limits ODCs to inference for now.
- Google's Trillium TPU showed no hard faults up to 15 krad, about 20× the expected 5-year shielded dose at 550 km.

**Bottom line:** The authors judge that ODCs are unlikely to be a meaningful share of compute before 2030. They could become cost-competitive within 3–5 years if Starship development stays on track, with chip production possibly becoming the bottleneck.

results:
The most relevant result is a November 13, 2026 MLex report that a California judge limited OpenAI's access to plaintiffs' medical histories in the suicide and psychological-harm suits. The search returned only a partial article, so I couldn't confirm the judge's name, the exact scope of the order, or the reasoning.

- **The ruling:** The judge said OpenAI's requests went too far and sided with plaintiffs, who argued they shouldn't have to disclose so much sensitive information before the court picks representative cases for bellwether trials.
- **What OpenAI sought:** According to the same report, OpenAI wanted years of medical histories, prescription medications and deeply personal experiences, including childhood trauma and abuse.
- **Ruling basis:** A separate summary of the same report says the judge found the proposed disclosures invasive and far beyond what was relevant.

Don't confuse this with the copyright litigation. Those results concern a different case, consolidated pretrial proceedings for 16 copyright lawsuits against OpenAI, in which Judge Stein affirmed an order requiring production of 20 million de-identified ChatGPT logs. That ruling is about user logs in copyright discovery, not the medical-history requests in the bellwether cases.

for f in "https://arstechnica.com/ai/feed/" "https://therecord.media/feed" "https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/feed/" "https://www.technologyreview.com/feed/" "https://huggingface.co/blog/feed.xml" "https://blogs.nvidia.com/feed/"; do echo "### $f"; curl -sS --max-time 25 "$f" | python3 -c "
import sys,re
t=sys.stdin.read()
items=re.findall(r'<(?:item|entry)>(.*?)</(?:item|entry)>',t,re.S)
for it in items[:12]:
    ti=re.search(r'<title[^>]*>(?:<!\[CDATA\[)?(.*?)(?:\]\]>)?</title>',it,re.S)
    pd=re.search(r'<(?:pubDate|published|updated)>(.*?)</',it,re.S)
    d=pd.group(1) if pd else '?'
    if '14 Nov 2026' in d or '15 Nov 2026' in d or '2026-11-14' in d or '2026-11-15' in d:
        li=re.search(r'<link[^>]*href=\"(.*?)\"|<link>(.*?)</link>',it,re.S)
        print(' ',d,'|',(ti.group(1).strip() if ti else '?'))
        if li: print('   ',li.group(1) or li.group(2))
" 2>/dev/null; done

results:
The search turned up consistent reporting that Nvidia's proposed OpenAI guarantee was cut roughly in half, with some disagreement on the final figure and timing.

- **The original proposal:** Nvidia had considered a $250 billion guarantee tied to an Ohio data center project where OpenAI planned to deploy about $300 billion of Nvidia chips. One of the largest proposals involved an Ohio data center project where OpenAI planned to deploy approximately $300 billion worth of NVIDIA chips. NVIDIA had considered providing a $250 billion financial guarantee to support the project.
- **Kress's role:** Colette Kress, now interim CEO, is reported to have pushed for the cut. Interim CEO Colette Kress reportedly spearheaded the guarantee reduction, a move previously resisted by Jensen Huang. Her role is described as a WSJ account, which I did not verify directly.
- **The final figure:** Nvidia's filings reportedly show the capped amount at $105 billion. According to NVIDIA's August 17 SEC filing, the final initial agreement capped its contingent guarantee obligations at $105 billion, covering approximately 4.25 gigawatts of data center capacity.
- **Conflicting figure:** One source puts the cap at about $125 billion for the same 4.25 GW, not $105 billion. Kress got the signed guarantee cap cut to about 4.25 gigawatts, or up to $125 billion. The $105 billion figure appears in more sources, but the discrepancy is unresolved here.
- **Timing:** The agreement is dated August 17 in several reports, while one morning brief says the reduction came prior to signing. That conflicts with the August 17 signing date, so treat the sequence as unclear.
- **Filing details:** One source notes that $105 billion covers credit support tied to OpenAI's leased campus in Ohio, and $3.5 billion covers data center leases for other AI cloud partners.

Most of these are single-outlet or newsletter sources, several of them amplifying the same WSJ report, so the $105 billion figure and the Kress attribution should be checked against Nvidia's own filings before relying on them.

[2611.11306] ScrapeBench: Evaluating Legal Compliance of AI Agents in Website Scraping

results:
The study is **ScrapeBench**, a paper on arXiv (2611.11306) that its listing says was accepted to NeurIPS 2026 (Evaluations and Datasets Track). Your "below 5%" figure is accurate but needs one qualifier: the paper reports that most agents exhibit low compliance rates (< 5%) when instructed to scrape websites in our sample of 1,626 popular websites that explicitly prohibit scraping. It is not a claim that every agent falls under 5%.

Other findings from the paper:
- **Checking the rules didn't fix it.** Agents that actively check the applicable ToS and robots.txt, they continue to exhibit low compliance rates.
- **Prompting changed the results.** Explicitly putting the ToS and robots.txt into the prompt made a difference. For Claude, explicit instructions and linking the policies raised compliance to 40.1% and 41.5%.
- **Over-refusal.** Some agents also refused lawful scraping tasks. The paper includes a human baseline with 180 participants, which reportedly showed compliance rates comparable to AI agents but over-refuse at much higher rates.

A secondary write-up (aiweekly) goes further than the arXiv text, saying that prompting the agent to read the policy first does not close the gap. That conflicts with the paper's own finding that explicit prompting raised Claude's compliance substantially, so the primary paper is the better source.

The search didn't turn up any FDA draft guidance on AI mental health chatbots dated November 2026. The results center on the November 2025 advisory committee meeting.

- **The committee meeting:** The Digital Health Advisory Committee met on November 6, 2025 to discuss generative AI-enabled digital mental health devices. It reviewed a hypothetical prescription large-language-model therapy chatbot for adults with major depressive disorder.
- **Recommendations:** Per one summary, the committee focused on phasing these tools in under clinician supervision and requiring sponsors to define serious adverse events, such as suicidal ideation, before deployment (psyreflect). Its recommendations are non-binding, and FDA generally follows such advice but is not legally bound to.
- **Status of follow-up:** One source from October 2026 says no second digital health advisory committee meeting has been scheduled or held, and that FDA has issued no guidance, draft or final, addressed to digital mental health as a category. This is a secondary source, so it should be checked against FDA's site.
- **Conflicting claim:** A TechInformed article refers to January guidance updates. I couldn't verify what those were, and they may refer to the general AI-enabled device lifecycle draft guidance rather than mental health specifically.

In summary, the paper introduces ScrapeBench, a benchmark for testing whether AI agents comply with website terms of service and robots.txt when scraping. It reports that most agents scraped sites that prohibit it at very low compliance rates, and that agents over-refused on sites that permit scraping. - **Over-refusal:** On the 269 permissive sites, Claude Opus 4.6 had an over-refusal rate of 98.5%.

The article is in the search results: Cao et al. (2026), "Cross-linguistic differences in responses to patient queries on osteonecrosis of the femoral head between English and Chinese-oriented large language models: a semantically matched bilingual cross-sectional study," published in Frontiers in Public Health, 14, Article 1985180.

- **Design:** The study compared three English-oriented models (ChatGPT-5.6-Sol, Gemini-3.1-Pro, and Claude-Fable-5) and three Chinese-oriented models (DeepSeek-V4-Pro, Qwen3.7-Max, and Doubao-Seed-2.1-Pro). The model names are as they appear in the search result.
- **Main findings:** The models differed significantly in actionability and clinical accuracy, but clinical accuracy demonstrated favorable cross-linguistic stability.
- **Readability:** None of the six-model outputs met the applicable readability threshold for patient-targeted health education under either language condition.
- **Interpretation:** The authors suggest that cross-LLM differences in Chinese-language readability arise, at least partially, from variation in linguistic expression rather than substantive differences in underlying semantic content.

The results don't include the full text, so I couldn't check the methods or the exact scoring tools.

Here's a brief summary of what the search turned up. None of the results are dated specifically to Sunday, November 15, 2026, and some pages are aggregators, so check the originals.

- **Frontier AI lawsuit (most recent):** Four nonprofits sued Anthropic, Google, Meta, OpenAI and SpaceXSI on November 12, 2026, seeking a freeze on increasingly advanced AI systems. The case was filed in San Francisco Superior Court under California's Unfair Competition Law. The plaintiffs acknowledge that a real freeze would require government inspections and monitoring.
- **Australia:** Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has announced a new artificial intelligence (AI) safety regulator, which will enforce penalties for frontier AI companies that breach their obligations. The government is also considering criminal law changes to deal with serious misconduct by any of these companies.
- **Kenya:** A High Court in Kerugoya directed the executive and parliament to finalise a legal and policy framework for AI within six months. The government said AI regulation is under way, citing a draft national policy published for public participation on 21 July 2026.
- **US federal and state:** One overview says as of 24 October 2026, we found no single US law that covers AI as a whole. Colorado signed SB 26-189, which replaces its 2024 AI law with rules for automated decision-making technology. The Justice Department joined a lawsuit by the AI company xAI against Colorado's 2024 AI law, arguing it violates the Equal Protection Clause.
- **Courts and AI-generated filings:** The Fifth Circuit decided not to adopt a proposed rule on the use of artificial intelligence in court filings, and one tracker counts 566 US court documents on generative AI and related AI questions as of 8 September 2026. A Law360 item reports that a federal judge questioned whether a Connecticut attorney's filings were affected by AI, with possible sanctions.

Source quality is mixed. The SafeLegalAI, JD Supra, and learnrudi pages are aggregators whose item lists look partly garbled, and at least one of the summaries contains unverified detail. The lawsuit and Australia items are the most recent, but I'd confirm them against primary reporting before relying on them.

# Tesla opens Cybercab pre-orders ‘for personal use,’ with geo restrictions and a $299 monthly fee

Tesla said on Friday evening that “select customers” now have the opportunity to pre-order the company’s autonomous, golden Cybercab “for personal use.”

More details became clear as those select customers looked at the order page. Tech reviewer Marques Brownlee posted that buyers “must accept delivery” in one of a handful of Texas cities and that the Cybercab will only operate in certain geofenced areas. The estimated delivery date is December 2026.

In addition to the $29,990 price tag, Cybercab owners will need to pay $299 per month to operate their vehicle.

In response to Brownlee’s post, Tesla CEO Elon Musk said the Cybercab “will be available nationwide, as we receive regulatory approval.” He added that the monthly fee is “too high”: “Should match the cost of Tesla [Full Self-Driving] and connectivity for other models, which is more like ~$115/month.”

Tesla’s Ashok Elluswamy offered more information about the geofencing, saying that Cybercab will work “unsupervised inside all the same geo locations as @robotaxi, just serving the owners’ needs.”

After falling far short of projected sales, Tesla recently announced it will cease Cybertruck production next year and use the additional factory capacity to build more Cybercabs.

HEADLINE: Petition to reinstate Jensen Huang passes 115,000 signatures as two investors press Nvidia board
PUBLISHED: TechCrunch — 1:41 PM PST, November 14, 2026; CNBC — November 14, 2026
SOURCES:
TechCrunch | https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/14/elon-musk-other-tech-execs-sign-petition-calling-on-nvidia-to-reinstate-jensen-huang/ | report
CNBC | https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/14/nvidia-investors-jensen-huang-return-board-letter.html | report
FACTS:
- TechCrunch says the petition "appears to have attracted more than 115,000 signatures as of Saturday afternoon"; the petition website lists signers including 5,965 current Nvidia employees, 1,108 former employees and 63,063 shareholders. Named supporters: Elon Musk, Replit's Amjad Masad, Epic's Tim Sweeney, Y Combinator's Garry Tan (TechCrunch).
- The petition says signers are "concerned that Jensen was removed without meaningful due process" and asks the board to "bring him back while an independent investigation establishes the facts" (TechCrunch).
- CNBC reports Altimeter Capital CEO Brad Gerstner posted a letter on X on Friday, co-signed by Atreides Management's Gavin Baker, urging Nvidia's board to "pursue a slow, measured, and deliberate process regarding the future leadership of Nvidia," including "the potential return of Jensen Huang." CNBC says the letter did not call for immediate reinstatement.
- CNBC: the two firms disclosed about $2.13 billion of Nvidia stock combined as of June 30 — Altimeter 9.4 million shares worth nearly $1.9 billion, Atreides 1.2 million shares worth nearly $250 million.
- CNBC adds that a separate letter sent Friday asked Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to testify about Megaspeed before the House Intelligence Committee, and that Lutnick has agreed to testify to the Senate Banking Committee on Dec. 10 on whether Commerce is "properly performing its broader role of preventing China from acquiring advanced AI chips."

Two major Nvidia shareholders are calling on the board of directors to weigh all options for the company's future leadership, including "the potential return of Jensen Huang."
Altimeter Capital CEO Brad Gerstner posted a letter on X on Friday that urges Nvidia's board to "pursue a slow, measured, and deliberate process regarding the future leadership of Nvidia." The letter is also signed by Atreides Management's Gavin Baker.

Nvidia was Altimeter Capital's largest disclosed equity holding in its most recent SEC filing , with a 9.4 million-share stake worth nearly $1.9 billion as of June 30. Atreides held 1.2 million shares worth nearly $250 million at the end of June.
The letter said Nvidia will be "capably led" by interim CEO Colette Kress , who served as Nvidia's CFO for 13 years before the board announced Thursday that she'd lead the company in Huang's absence.
"But the Founder and long time incredible leader of this extraordinary company has earned the right for a deliberate process that avoids any needless rush to replace him before all the facts are known," the letter concludes. The document did not call for Huang's immediate reinstatement.

#
How the Nvidia scandal lifted the curtain on a loophole that’s giving China access to US chips

By Stephanie Yang

Updated Nov 15, 2026, 5:30 AM ET

PUBLISHED Nov 14, 2026, 10:00 AM ET

People walk across Jubilee bridge at Marina Bay in Singapore on May 5, 2026.

Roslan Rahman/AFP/Getty Images

Headquartered in a curved glass skyscraper that boasts commanding views over Singapore’s Marina Bay district, Megaspeed International is just the type of fast-growing tech start-up that Asia’s wealthy city-state has been keen to attract.

In three years, the corporate entity has gone from an inactive Chinese gaming subsidiary to one of Asia’s biggest buyers of cutting-edge semiconductors from the US.

But its rapid rise has also propelled it to the center of an alleged spy scandal that’s now engulfing Nvidia , the $4 trillion company behind the world’s most advanced chips.

At the same time, suspicions that Megaspeed may be exploiting a loophole in US export controls is exacerbating a rift within the US government on how to best keep China from accessing its most sensitive technologies.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned on Thursday after admitting to having an affair. Congress has also called on him to testify behind closed doors about his romantic relationship with Alice Huang, no relation, whom US officials believe to be a Chinese intelligence asset. Beijing has said the claim is a “groundless” attempt to smear China.

Also known as Huang Le , the 43-year-old Chinese executive played an integral role in establishing Megaspeed, according to corporate documents and media reports. CNN has made continued efforts to reach her for comment.

But as Megaspeed quietly instilled billions of dollars of Nvidia chips in data centers across Southeast Asia, it came under the scrutiny of the Singaporean government, as well as US officials concerned that the company was passing those chips on to unauthorized Chinese buyers.

“Chips are the absolute ground-zero of all other technology,” said Alex Capri, a senior lecturer in the business school at the National University of Singapore. “The appetite for Nvidia’s chips in China is absolutely insatiable… Nvidia chips are still far and away the best.”

But US export controls have fettered Chinese access to its most advanced semiconductor technology, spawning a shadow industry of complex transactions, shell companies and chip smuggling – of which Megaspeed is now under suspicion by US authorities and lawmakers of helping enable.

CNN

Nvidia’s CEO is out after 33 years. What’s next?

On Thursday, Megaspeed CEO Tan Yong Pong said in a statement the company has cooperated with inspections by the US Department of Commerce and has retained a US law firm to independently verify its compliance with export controls.

“Megaspeed takes its compliance obligations under US export control laws extremely seriously. Compliance is a fundamental priority for the company, and Megaspeed is committed to working constructively and transparently with the US government,” the statement said.

In a new statement on Sunday, Megaspeed said that Huang left the company on August 30, 2025, and currently holds no role there.

“Megaspeed is aware of recent media reports containing assertions about our business, supply chain and global operations that are not supported by verifiable evidence,” the statement said.

The logo of data center company Megaspeed International is pictured at its office in the Ocean Financial Centre in Singapore on November 10, 2026.

Taryn NG/AFP/Getty Images

#
A billion-dollar business

In 2022, the US began restricting sales of semiconductors to China, including Nvidia’s most advanced. While the controls were meant to curb China’s tech industry, they also spawned opportunities for intermediaries willing to help circumvent them.

US officials believe Megaspeed may be one of those.

Incorporated in 2015 as 7Road International, an offshoot of a Chinese gaming company, the company’s name changed to Megaspeed in March 2023, and Alice Huang became a director through November of that year. Since then, trade records show Megaspeed has purchased more than $4 billion in chips and equipment from Nvidia.

Capri, who also wrote the book, “Techno-Nationalism: How It’s Reshaping Trade, Geopolitics and Society,” said Megaspeed’s business model, in which it builds data centers and rents out its computing services, gives Chinese companies another point of access to advanced US chips.

“If you put me on the restricted list to drive a Ferrari, and I say ‘Okay, well I can’t buy a Ferrari, I can’t import a Ferrari, but I can just go to a car dealership and rent a Ferrari,’ right? And do whatever I want with the Ferrari,” he said. “That’s an issue. It’s the car dealership that you have to control.”

The orange Alibaba logo is displayed on the sunlit glass facade of the Shenzhen Alibaba Center on November 11, in Shenzhen, Guangdong Province, China.

Cheng Xin/Getty Images

Corporate filings show connections between subsidiary entities of Megaspeed

response.stdout:
Corporate filings show connections between subsidiary entities of Megaspeed and Chinese e-commerce giant Alibaba, including the pledging of collateral. CNN has sought comment from Alibaba.

In other cases, Chinese buyers have been able to procure sensitive components of their own, often done through a web of ghost corporations and brokers through which the chips – sometimes concealed in other electronics or containers – can reach end users in China, experts said.

Based on indictments and investigative reports, research institute Epoch AI estimates that anywhere between 290,000 to 1.6 million advanced US semiconductors were sent to China in violation of export controls last year.

“This is a pipeline that has developed that benefits from the fact that there is minimal scrutiny on US air data, that you can bring things into Singapore, Malaysia, Central and Southeast Asia and then move those goods, sometimes through Thailand, into China,” trade data investigator William George told CNN.

“It is incredibly hard to look at this and not see a Chinese state-sponsored network for bypassing US export control networks,” he said.

Singapore also initiated investigations into Megaspeed and its controllers, including Alice Huang, for potential false declarations relating to the company’s server purchases and their final destinations.

In a statement, Singapore’s Ministry of Home Affairs said there was insufficient evidence Huang that had committed any related offenses, but she had been barred from re-entering the country after providing inaccurate information “to downplay her role” at Megaspeed. The other investigations are ongoing.

#
Closing the loopholes

The exact scale of Chinese chip smuggling is impossible to quantify. However, its existence has become something of an open secret in the industry, as well as an indication that US efforts to keep adversaries from securing high-stakes technology still have fundamental flaws.

A May report from the short seller Culper Research claimed that despite tightening trade restrictions, Chinese end-users still account for about 20% of Nvidia chip sales via illegal diversion and intermediaries in Southeast Asia.

Jensen Huang, who has accompanied US President Donald Trump to events with Chinese leader Xi Jinping twice this year, has lobbied for the US to relax controls on Chinese chip imports. The US government ultimately approved several buyers for less-advanced Nvidia chips, known as H200, while collecting a quarter of the revenue.

Eric and Lara Trump, SpaceX, Twitter and electric car maker Tesla CEO Elon Musk (C), US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, US Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth and Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang walk off Air Force One upon arriving at Beijing Capital Airport in Beijing on May 13.

Brendan Smialowski/AFP/ Getty Images

However, blacklisted companies have continued to obtain sensitive semiconductors as well.

They include Northwestern Polytechnical University, based in Xi’an, the capital of China’s Shaanxi province, one of the nation’s leading universities with military ties, known collectively as the “Seven Sons of National Defense.”

Northwestern Polytechnical University has been on the US Department of Commerce’s Entity List since 2001, yet it bought four H200 chips last month for $250,000, according to procurement records published on its own website that have since been deleted.

Northwestern Polytechnical University did not respond to a phone call from CNN seeking comment.

Despite investigation by the US, Megaspeed has not been labeled a national security threat or subject to limitations on chip purchases — a decision by Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick that led to a confrontation by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent last week, two people familiar with the matter told CNN.

Meanwhile, Democratic lawmakers, whose party recently won control of the House and Senate, are calling for greater oversight for US exports of advanced chips, days before Trump’s due to meet Xi for the third time this year in the Chinese tech hub of Shenzhen.

A growing number of chip smuggling cases has fueled calls for harsher legal enforcement outside the US as well. The Taiwanese government is seeking to criminalize unauthorized exports of advanced AI chips to China, as prosecutors there charged nine people in a scheme to sneak Nvidia chips into China through Japan, Indonesia and Hong Kong.

“There’s going to have to be new standards that are going to have to be enforced around traceability and transparency,” Capri said. “This is really going to be the beginning of a major crackdown, and actually moving on to the next phase of export control enforcement.”

CNN’s Yong Xiong, Isaac Yee and Wayne Chang contributed reporting.

I found no coverage dated November 14, 2026, so I can't confirm any news from that day. The results cover the GUARD Act, the Hawley-Blumenthal bill on AI companions and minors.

- **Bill contents:** The bill would prohibit AI companions for users under the age of 18 and require these systems to disclose their "non-human status and lack of professional credentials" for all users. Age verification is also part of it, and it makes it a criminal offense to make publicly available a chatbot that engages minors in sexually explicit content or solicits them to commit self-harm or violence, with fines up to $250,000 per offense.
- **Committee action:** A Roll Call article dated April 30, 2026 reports that a bill that would require age verification and ban minors from companion chatbots advanced unanimously in a Senate committee. The bill now awaits consideration by the full Senate.
- **Duty of care:** A Tech Policy Press analysis says neither bill establishes an affirmative safety standard, and both create procedural obligations or safeguards such as consent, controls, verification, and disclosures. So the GUARD Act does not appear to impose a duty of care.
- **Opposition:** Free speech and privacy groups have objected to the age-verification requirement. One of them argued that mandating government ID or equivalent age verification for any American who wishes to interact with an AI chatbot burdens the speech and associational rights of every adult.

The results do not say whether a full Senate vote is scheduled. Some dates in the metadata conflict, so the April 2026 committee date is the most reliable one I found.

input.prompt: Give the publication date. Report the facts with exact quotes and figures: what the UN conference is, dates, who said what about lethal autonomous weapons, the 1,000 targets per day claim, national positions, and any Amodei quote.

response.result:
**Publication date:** Sunday, November 15, 2026 (Taipei Times, page 5, AFP dispatch from Paris)

**The UN conference:** The article says a conference starting "tomorrow" at the UN in Geneva will discuss curbs and prohibitions on lethal autonomous weapons systems (LAWS). That would make the start date November 16, 2026, though the article does not state it. The talks take place under the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons. Some analysts doubt the talks can keep pace with the technology.

**Definition:** Geneva Centre for Security Policy head Jean-Marc Rickli said LAWS "can identify, select, and engage a target without the intervention of a human operator in the execution of these tasks."

**Key issue:** Regulators must decide the level of human control over the decision to use such a weapon.

**National positions:**
- **US:** Refers to "appropriate levels of human judgement" in using autonomous weapons.
- **France:** Bans LAWS but permits "partially autonomous" systems, which it calls PLAWS. Rear Adm. Vincent Sebastien, deputy director of the French Ministry of Defense's Agency for Defence Artificial Intelligence, said human control is ensured through "appropriate control" by a military commander, a concept whose scope varies by system and context.

**Officials and analysts:**
- **UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres and ICRC president Mirjana Spoljaric** (joint statement, August): "We are now dangerously close to crossing a moral red line: the autonomous targeting of humans by machines." They also said a race toward greater autonomy is "already well underway."
- **Rickli** called the Geneva agenda "very narrow," adding that it "fails to encompass the full range of issues surrounding AI on the battlefield."
- **Laure de Roucy-Rochegonde** (French Institute of International Relations) warned of "a host of problems and unacceptable risks" in targeting and decision-support systems.
- **Sebastien** said: "Autonomy will very quickly become a reality on the battlefield."

**The 1,000 targets claim:** Rickli cited the US-Israeli war against Iran this year, saying "the Americans engaged as many as 1,000 targets per day" inside Iran. The article reports this claim without independent verification.

**Deployment:** The autonomous weapons under discussion are not yet in widespread use. Analysts said they have been deployed by Russia in Ukraine and in US attacks in Iran.

**Swarms:** Rickli said drone swarms, which "aim to neutralize an adversary through saturation," would be highly effective, and some states see them as a crucial strategic advantage.

**Anthropic cofounder Dario Amodei:** "Today, frontier AI systems are simply not reliable enough to power fully autonomous weapons." The article also says that significant doubts and dangers remain and that the incentive for major powers is too strong to stop development.

# US disrupts North Korean campaign behind $400 million crypto theft

By

# Bill Toulas

- November 14, 2026

- 10:15 AM

- 0



The U.S. government has disrupted a North Korean social engineering campaign called ‘FaceStealer’, responsible for stealing more than $400 million in cryptocurrency.



The attacks used multiple social engineering techniques, including deepfakes and ClickFix, to target individuals in the cryptocurrency and Web3 sectors, as well as open-source developers.



The FaceStealer campaign ran for 18 months before the U.S. seized the underlying cloud-based infrastructure.



U.S. authorities identified more than 900 webcam videos that hackers secretly recorded of tech workers, who were deceived in the massive North Korean operation.



An FBI alert earlier this week notes that the North Korean threat actor hijacked accounts on Telegram, LinkedIn, Slack, and Discord, and used them to invite victims to video meetings under various pretenses.



During the video calls, the attacker showed recorded footage of people the targets knew and who had previously fallen victim, too.



The FBI explains that while the target waited for the meeting to start, the hacker secretly recorded a video, which was later used with other targets. The meeting sometimes featured recordings of multiple familiar individuals to add pressure on the current victim in the next stage.



Shortly after, the hacker claimed a technical issue and displayed a fake error message to justify delivering a malicious “fix.”



The target was then prompted to follow a link that purported to offer a fix, such as an update or installer, which infected their computer with malware that steals crypto data and account credentials for video meeting platforms such as Zoom, Google Meet, and Microsoft Teams.



The malware also provides access to the victims' contact lists, social media, communication apps, and webcam videos.





Infection cycle

Source: FBI





According to the FBI, attackers sometimes delayed targeting individuals for months or even more than a year after the initial compromise, likely waiting for their cryptocurrency holdings to grow.



ArticWolf researchers attributed the FaceStealer campaign to the BlueNoroff hacker group and listed additional lures , including financial documents, fake PDF viewer updates, identity verification prompts, and security audits, all designed to persuade the target to run a “fix.”



The researchers identified 677 targets across 58 countries, with a heavy focus on company founders and senior executives.





Tools North Korean hackers used to create malicious videos

Source: ArticWolf





Huntress cybersecurity company attributed a similar campaign to BlueNoroff in 2025, where the attackers used Zoom calls to infect company executives with custom macOS malware.



The FBI bulletin highlighted an incident in which the hackers compromised the maintainer of a popular open-source JavaScript library with tens of millions of weekly downloads, after luring them into a fake Teams meeting with multiple participants, including one familiar to the developer.



The attack was thwarted thanks to quick detection, but the FBI says it confirmed multiple other attempts against developers in the npm and Rust crate ecosystems.



Amazon threat analysts also attributed several open-source software supply chain attacks to BlueNoroff in a July 2026 report .



To defend against these attacks, users are recommended to join meetings only through official apps using an invite code, verify unexpected invitations independently, and keep the webcam off unless explicitly needed. Finally, avoid running scripts offered as fixes to technical problems.



As a separate announcement, the U.S. Justice Department said that together with private sector companies, the U.S. government froze more than $2.7 billion from the 6.4 billion Binance crypto heist .



The DoJ has already "obtained court-authorization to seize or restrain in excess of $1.2 billion of that amount."

SECTION: Health, science & medicine
HEADLINE: npj Digital Medicine publishes stroke CT/MRI model reporting AUROC 0.974 on 6,650-patient CT cohort
PUBLISHED: Published online: 14 November 2026 (npj Digital Medicine)
SOURCES:
npj Digital Medicine | https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-03458-9 | primary
FACTS:
- The paper describes the Dynamic Fuzzy Encoder Network (DFE-Net), which "uses learnable fuzzy membership fields to represent spatial uncertainty and jointly classify stroke and localize lesions," per the abstract.
- Evaluated on "a multicentre computed tomography (CT) cohort comprising 6650 patients and 8873 images and a separate magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) cohort comprising 67 patients and 615 images"; training and testing were done separately within each modality.
- Reported results: "area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.974 and an F1 score of 0.897 on CT, and corresponding values of 0.978 and 0.879 on MRI." CT lesion localization against expert annotations gave "a Dice score of 0.70."
- Expected calibration error was "~0.022 in both cohorts" and the model "contained 0.20 million parameters." The authors state "prospective validation and expert-annotated MRI evaluation remain necessary"; MRI localization used "gradient-derived pseudo-targets because expert lesion masks were unavailable." No comparator model is named in the abstract.
- Authors are at Wenzhou Medical University, TU Munich, Hunan Medical College, Ningbo University, Huashan Hospital/Fudan and UCL; the paper states "The authors received no specific funding for this work."
FLAGS: (none)

The authors limit their conclusion to "radiologist-supervised retrospective quantitative research within the evaluated cohorts."

Learning uncertainty fields for joint brain stroke diagnosis and intrinsic lesion localization in CT and MRI

Download PDF

# Abstract
Early stroke changes can be difficult to detect and localize on neuroimaging, particularly when lesion boundaries are indistinct. We developed the Dynamic Fuzzy Encoder Network (DFE-Net), which uses learnable fuzzy membership fields to represent spatial uncertainty and jointly classify stroke and localize lesions. We evaluated the model on a multicentre computed tomography (CT) cohort comprising 6650 patients and 8873 images and a separate magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) cohort comprising 67 patients and 615 images. Training and testing were performed separately within each modality. DFE-Net achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.974 and an F1 score of 0.897 on CT, and corresponding values of 0.978 and 0.879 on MRI. In the CT cohort, lesion localization against expert annotations yielded a Dice score of 0.70. MRI localization was assessed using gradient-derived pseudo-targets because expert lesion masks were unavailable. Expected calibration error was ~0.022 in both cohorts, and the model contained 0.20 million parameters. These results support joint diagnosis and spatial localization with a compact model, while prospective validation and expert-annotated MRI evaluation remain necessary.

# Abstract
Automated breast dynamic contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (DCE-MRI) segmentation could facilitate quantitative tumor measurement, but geometric overlap alone does not establish the fidelity of mask-derived measurements. We developed an enhancement-aware three-dimensional MedNeXt framework with gated skip fusion and boundary supervision and evaluated it in a retrospective multi-cohort design spanning locked internal testing, source-held-out assessment, retrospective external validation, and radiologist review. Measurement fidelity was the primary endpoint. Across 521 paired internal-test and DUKE cases, median errors were 9.7% for tumor volume, 1.8 mm for 3D maximum surface diameter, and 10.2% for operational enhancement-defined volume, with corresponding ICCs of 0.97, 0.80, and 0.97. Median Dice was 0.831 internally and 0.823 in the DUKE source-held-out stratum, and was 0.812 and 0.806 in the BC-MRI-SEG and public BreastDCEDL_AMBL retrospective external-validation cohorts, respectively, using the frozen checkpoint without external-label tuning. No major correction was required for 78 of 80 masks in the blinded two-reader review. In 276 paired response-analysis cases, AUROC was 0.732 with automatic geometry and 0.757 with expert geometry (difference, −0.025; 95% CI, −0.095 to 0.045); discrimination non-inferiority was not demonstrated. These findings support automated segmentation as a starting point for radiologist-supervised retrospective quantitative research within the evaluated cohorts, while distinguishing measurement fidelity from downstream predictive equivalence.

# Abstract
Learning Health Systems (LHSs) use routinely collected data to generate evidence that informs practice through continuous learning cycles. Artificial intelligence (AI) and data science may strengthen this model, but how LHS frameworks and AI applications relate remains unclear. We mapped LHS frameworks and their components and examined how AI and data science are integrated. Searches identified U.S.-based, English-language studies published January 2007–August 2025; two reviewers independently screened and extracted data, resolving disagreements by consensus. We included 54 framework studies (24 [44%] conceptual adaptations; 30 [56%] real-world implementations) and 30 AI/data science studies. Five components recurred across the frameworks: data infrastructure and interoperability, governance and stakeholder engagement, learning and improvement cycles, evidence generation and translation, and equity and ethics. Relative to framework studies, AI studies less often addressed governance and stakeholder engagement (17% vs 35%) or equity (13% vs 22%), emphasizing computational over organizational functions. Most AI studies (27/30) focused on the data-to-knowledge phase; only three extended to knowledge-to-practice, and none described practice-to-data feedback with post-deployment outcomes informing model updating. AI applications capture only part of the LHS vision, concentrating on knowledge generation with less attention to the organizational and feedback mechanisms needed to translate insights into practice and sustain learning.

# Marcos signs EO forming National AI Council

-

Duey Guison

-

November 15, 2026

President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. has signed Executive Order (EO) No. 131, establishing the National AI Council (NAIC). The council will serve as the government’s primary guide for AI-related policy development, regulatory conditions, institutional growth, and capacity building.

Under the EO, Executive Secretary Ralph Recto will chair the council, with Department of Economy, Planning, and Development (DEPDev) Secretary Arsenio Balisacan serving as vice chairperson and the council’s secretariat. Other members include the heads of the DOST, DICT, DTI, DOF, DepEd, DOLE, DBM, CHED, and TESDA, alongside a single representative from the private sector. The private-sector appointee will serve a three-year term and may be reappointed once.

While we recognize the administration’s intent in forming a dedicated body to guide the country’s AI policies, we have serious reservations about the council’s leadership and composition. Both Recto and Balisacan are economists by training, raising valid questions about their technical expertise when it comes to governing fast-evolving AI technologies.

Aside from that, limiting the private sector to just a single representative feels shortsighted. Given that private enterprises and tech practitioners are driving AI innovation on the ground, the council would benefit from broader representation of seasoned AI experts rather than relying heavily on traditional economic managers.

Those reservations aside, we hope the National AI Council succeeds in implementing and refining the Philippines’ AI Governance Framework.

Every flagged caveat (company-claim, single-source, preprint, update) is voiced somewhere in its block. Numbers check out digit-for-digit with the exceptions below.

1. SCRIPT LINE: "There is one paper worth the number." (Research block, host A) — and the preceding "Research is thin today".
CLOSEST EDITION TEXT: the "Research & papers" section contains two items: "Preprint reports 5.85x decoding speedup for looped transformers…" and "Open SLAM recipe cuts egocentric trajectory error from 1.02 m to 0.43 m but still trails Meta's closed Aria system overall".
WRONG: editorial characterisation that contradicts the edition — the edition carries a second research paper (SLAM Dunk, submitted 15 Nov, with reported results). "Worth the number" is a value judgment the edition does not make. ("arXiv ran no announcement cycle inside our window" is itself supported.)

2. SCRIPT LINE: "Megaspeed started out in 2015 as 7Road International… and was renamed in March 2023." / "CNN says trade records show it has since purchased more than $4 billion in chips and equipment from Nvidia."
CLOSEST EDITION TEXT: "renamed Megaspeed in March 2023, and that Alice Huang became a director through November of that year; 'Since then, trade records show Megaspeed has purchased more than $4 billion in chips and equipment from Nvidia.'" — and summary: "has bought more than $4 billion… since November 2023".
WRONG: changed baseline. The edition's "since then" anchors to November 2023 (Huang's directorship); the script drops that clause so "since" anchors to the March 2023 renaming, shifting the start of the $4bn window by eight months.

3. SCRIPT LINE: "CNN has the clearest account yet of the mechanism."
CLOSEST EDITION TEXT: "The mechanism at issue is renting rather than exporting…"
WRONG: editorial/comparative claim ("clearest account yet") that the edition does not contain.

4. SCRIPT LINE: "Cursor says fewer than 0.05% of users had traces exposed and fewer than 0.01% had credentials compromised"
CLOSEST EDITION TEXT: "fewer than 0.05% of users had coding-agent traces exposed and fewer than 0.01% of customers had API credentials compromised"
WRONG: baseline changed — the edition's second figure is a share of *customers*, not users; the script's elision reads as "users" for both.

5. SCRIPT LINE: "Cursor estimates up to 5,000 users may have received them." (and intro: "let attackers push malicious copies of Anthropic's Claude Code extension to as many as 5,000 developers")
CLOSEST EDITION TEXT: "Cursor estimates up to 5,000 users who requested affected versions may have received the malicious builds"; summary: "exposing up to 5,000 developers to a persistent SSH backdoor".
WRONG: the scope qualifier "who requested affected versions" is dropped, broadening the population; the intro's "push… to as many as 5,000 developers" also asserts delivery where the summary says "exposing".

6. SCRIPT LINE: "So the measurement is sound." / "The measurement is sound. The prediction is not."
CLOSEST EDITION TEXT: "The authors limit their conclusion to 'radiologist-supervised retrospective quantitative research within the evaluated cohorts', explicitly 'distinguishing measurement fidelity from downstream predictive equivalence'."
WRONG: verdict ("sound") the edition does not render; the edition reports fidelity metrics and the authors' explicit refusal to generalise, not a judgment that measurement is sound.

7. SCRIPT LINE: "CNN also carries an Epoch AI estimate that anywhere between 290,000 to 1.6 million advanced US semiconductors were sent to China…"
CLOSEST EDITION TEXT: "CNN cites Epoch AI's estimate, based on indictments and investigative reports, that 'anywhere between 290,000 to 1.6 million…'"
WRONG: the methodological qualifier "based on indictments and investigative reports" is dropped, presenting the range as an unqualified estimate.

8. SCRIPT LINE: "CNBC reports that Altimeter's Brad Gerstner posted a letter… urging Nvidia's board to pursue a slow, measured, and deliberate process… including the potential return of Jensen Huang."
CLOSEST EDITION TEXT: "CNBC says the letter did not call for immediate reinstatement and described the company as 'capably led' by interim CEO Colette Kress, who was CFO for 13 years."
WRONG: the limiting qualifier CNBC attaches to the letter is dropped entirely, leaving the ask stronger than the edition states.

9. SCRIPT LINE: "averaged across a set of reasoning and coding benchmarks"
CLOSEST EDITION TEXT: "averaged across seven benchmarks: GSM8K, MATH-500, BBH, HumanEval+, MBPP+, SpecBench and Spider"
WRONG: characterises the benchmark set in a way the edition does not — SpecBench (speculative decoding) and Spider (text-to-SQL) are not described as reasoning or coding benchmarks; the count "seven" is also replaced with a vague "a set".

10. SCRIPT LINE: "The MRI arm is small, and the paper says so."
CLOSEST EDITION TEXT: "The MRI arm is small and weakly supervised: the paper states 'MRI localization was assessed using gradient-derived pseudo-targets because expert lesion masks were unavailable'…"
WRONG: attribution shifted — "the MRI arm is small" is the edition's own framing; the quoted paper statement is about pseudo-targets, not about cohort size.

11. SCRIPT LINE: "TechCrunch says that on top of the $29,990 price… buyers must accept delivery in one of a handful of Texas cities."
CLOSEST EDITION TEXT: "It cites Marques Brownlee's post that buyers 'must accept delivery' in one of a handful of Texas cities and that the car will only operate in certain geofenced areas."
WRONG: attribution changed — the edition sources the Texas-delivery and geofence detail to Brownlee's post as cited by TechCrunch, not to TechCrunch's own reporting. The script's following "And it only drives inside a geofence?" / "It does." likewise states it flatly.

12. SCRIPT LINE (intro): "CNN reported that the Singapore data centre company Megaspeed has bought more than $4 billion in chips and equipment from Nvidia"
CLOSEST EDITION TEXT: "Singapore-based Megaspeed has bought more than $4 billion…" / "Megaspeed's model of building data centres and renting out computing services"
WRONG: minor characterisation — the edition says "Singapore-based" and describes a business model; it never labels Megaspeed a "data centre company". The intro also drops the summary's "since November 2023" (see #2).

13. SCRIPT LINE: "copied data from a storage bucket the two companies shared"
CLOSEST EDITION TEXT: "used it to copy data from a read-only storage bucket Cursor shared with Fireworks"
WRONG: drops "read-only", a qualifier bounding the access the key gave.
